extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy and epistemology (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for judging moral actions (three measures: divine law, civil law, reputation) and for assessing the clarity/distinctness of ideas; includes causes of obscurity/confusion and remedies. Useful for analyzing moral judgments and the precision of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of God (Divine law) as moral measure
rubrics_metrics.description: When we take the rule from the will of a supreme invisible Lawgiver, actions commanded or forbidden by God are called good or evil, sin or duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conformity to the divine will as the touchstone: if an action is supposed commanded by God it is called good; if forbidden, evil. This is presented as one of three possible standards by which men judge moral rectitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of politic societies (Civil law) as moral measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule made by the legislative power of the country (commonwealth) measures actions as lawful or unlawful, a crime or no crime; the commonwealth has power to enforce it and to punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by their agreement with municipal statutes and the enforcement mechanisms (rewards/punishments) ready to hand; when compared to civil law an action is denominated lawful or unlawful regardless of other standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of opinion or reputation (Law of fashion) as moral measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue and vice are often attributed according to what actions are in reputation or discredit in a country or society — virtue is that which has allowance of public esteem and vice that which has blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that private censure, commendation, and fashion operate as a rule: reputational incentives (praise/dislike) enforce conformity. This explains why people typically act to maintain reputation even when they disregard divine or civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue equals what is thought praiseworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: That this is the common MEASURE of virtue and vice: Virtue is everywhere that which is thought praiseworthy; nothing else but that which has the allowance of public esteem is called virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about virtue, check whether the action is publicly esteemed in that society; note cultural variation but also the general alignment with broader notions of right and wrong due to common self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral relations: conformity of voluntary actions to a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality is the relation of voluntary actions to these rules: an action's moral goodness or evil consists in its conformity or nonconformity to the rule taken as measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge moral rectitude by comparing the simple ideas composing the action to the pattern prescribed by the chosen rule (divine, civil, or reputational).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish positive/absolute ideas from relative (moral) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions may be regarded either absolutely (as positive mixed modes) or in relation (as good, bad, or indifferent depending on conformity to a rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, separate the descriptive account of an action (its positive idea, e.g., 'duelling') from its moral evaluation relative to a chosen rule (it may be valour in fashion, sin by divine law, or a capital crime by civil law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading denominations (names conflating mode and moral judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the same name often expresses both the positive idea of an action and its moral relation, people are apt to be misled into condemning actions solely by their name (e.g., 'stealing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer moral gravity from the label alone; examine the action's relation to the relevant rule(s). Example: taking a sword from a madman is denominated 'stealing' as a mode but need not be a sin relative to God's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: All relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations (including moral relations) are ultimately founded on simple ideas received from sensation or reflection; complex relational judgments resolve into comparisons of simple ideas (e.g., sweetness, generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing relational claims, trace them back to the simple ideas that compose the relevant concepts to see whether the relation holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation is perceivable whether the rule is true or false
rubrics_metrics.description: One can perceive an action's agreement or disagreement with a rule regardless of whether that rule is true; measuring by a wrong rule still yields a relation though may yield a mistaken moral judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between (a) the relation of action to a given rule (detectable) and (b) the correctness of the rule itself (a separate inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear versus obscure ideas (definition by sight analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear ideas are like objects in good light (presented as they were taken); obscure ideas lack original exactness or have faded and are not presented with the same freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity by whether the idea can be readily produced by memory or perception; obscurity arises from dull organs, slight impressions, or weak memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct versus confused ideas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A DISTINCT idea is one in which the mind perceives a difference from all other ideas; a CONFUSED idea is one not sufficiently distinguishable from another from which it ought to differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the idea contains perceivable differences that separate it from other ideas; lack of such differences indicates confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of confusion: complex ideas made of too few simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea composed of too small a number of simple ones, especially common ones, lacks the differences that make it deserve a different name (e.g., a bare idea of 'a beast with spots' is an insufficient idea of 'leopard').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure complex concepts include enough distinguishing simple ideas to be separable from neighboring concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of confusion: ingredients jumbled disorderly
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the number of simple ideas is sufficient, if they are so jumbled together that it is not discernible whether the idea belongs more to one name than another, the idea is confused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order and structure the components of a complex idea so that it clearly maps to the intended name; examples include misleading pictures that lack discernible order until properly transformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of confusion: mutable/undetermined simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person changes the idea they attach to a term from one occasion to another, the idea becomes uncertain and thus confused (e.g., varying ideas of 'church' or 'idolatry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix a steady combination of simple ideas under a given name; avoid altering the constituents each time you use the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion always concerns two ideas — identify what it's confounded with
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion implies difficulty separating two things that should be separated; whenever an idea is suspected to be confused, examine the other idea it is in danger of being confounded with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose confusion by finding the proximate neighboring idea that lacks sufficient distinction; work to identify whether the idea is the same, part of, or as properly called by that other name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy: unite precise ingredients and apply the same name steadily
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent confusion, collect and unite into one complex idea as precisely as possible all the ingredients that differentiate it from others, and apply the same name steadily to that determinate idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful definition, steady usage, and precise composition of simple ideas to maintain distinctness; this is both a methodological and linguistic prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas may be distinct in one part and confused in another
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea can be very distinct in one component while very obscure or confused in another (e.g., chiliaedron: clear idea of the number 'thousand' but confused idea of its figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning, attend to which part of a complex idea your arguments rely on; avoid inferring properties about the obscure parts from the clear parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of obscurity: dull organs, slight impressions, weak memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity in simple ideas arises from inadequate sensory input (dull organs), transient or slight impressions, or weakness in memory failing to retain the original exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sensory conditions and memory reliability when judging whether an idea is clear; improving sensory conditions or strengthening memory/attention may remedy obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of clear distinct ideas for infinite concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: We lack clear, distinct ideas of actual infinities (e.g., eternity or infinitely divisible matter); we have clear ideas of number and division in general, but not of the whole extent of an endless duration or actual infinitely small parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious reasoning about infinities: much that appears clear (e.g., duration, infinite divisibility) actually rests on obscure, undetermined parts and returns to numerical addability rather than a distinct idea of actual infinite parts.
